briefings.title: Synthetic users: useful for ideas, unproven for measurement
briefings.dek: Teams must decide which research tasks can go to AI stand-ins and which still need real participants and human judgment.
briefings.scenario: A product team at a large retailer has a tight budget and a long recruitment queue. They are considering AI-simulated users to shape early concepts, predict usability scores, and sort thousands of open-ended survey comments that nobody has time to read.

positions.label: Use for early exploration
positions.summary: Nielsen's roundups present simulated users as a way to widen early design thinking, involve more perspectives, and help designers reason through usage. He also warns that their feedback skews too positive, so they suit divergent thinking better than verdicts.

positions.label: Test against human benchmarks
positions.summary: MeasuringU treats replacement as a claim to check. It compares digital-twin predictions of SUS scores with real results, and it revisits whether ChatGPT can code open-ended survey comments as well as human researchers. The excerpts name the cost and speed appeal but do not show the outcomes.

briefings.context: Recruitment is slow and expensive, and open-ended survey comments are often skimmed or skipped, so both simulated participants and automated coding are tempting. The sources cover two kinds of use. One is generative, where a flawed simulation can still prompt useful thinking. The other is evaluative, where the output stands in for a measurement and errors or flattery matter more.

steps.label: Sort by purpose
steps.text: Label each planned AI use as idea generation or as evidence for a decision, and allow synthetic participants only for the first.

steps.label: Run a human check
steps.text: Before trusting automated coding or predicted scores, compare them with human-coded or real-participant results from a past study.

steps.label: Watch for flattery
steps.text: Read simulated feedback with the expectation that it is too agreeable, and confirm any usability concern or approval with real users.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts do not report how accurate digital twins or ChatGPT coding turned out to be, so the validity of either use is not settled here.

briefings.title: Is AI quietly eroding designers' core skills?
briefings.dek: Teams must decide whether to treat deskilling as a real threat to judgment and taste, or as a fear built on weak evidence.
briefings.scenario: A design org at a large retailer has rolled out AI tools and agents across its product teams, and output has climbed sharply. A lead wonders whether junior designers are still building the judgment to tell good work from merely plausible work, and whether to limit tool use or leave things alone.

positions.label: Erosion is already happening
positions.summary: Several writers argue that handing thinking to AI weakens skills, that taste is hard to develop in today's tools and risk-averse culture, and that running many agents at once makes it harder to see work as a whole.

positions.label: Evidence is overstated
positions.summary: Jakob Nielsen's roundup holds that most deskilling research looks at the wrong condition, so its findings should not be taken as proof that designers are losing ability.

briefings.context: Taste, judgment and holistic view are often named as the human strengths that last as AI takes over production. The pieces here ask whether current working conditions let designers keep building those strengths. The disagreement is partly about evidence: first-person and cultural arguments on one side, a critique of study design on the other.

steps.label: Audit your own use
steps.text: Note where your team lets AI make judgment calls versus where it only speeds up execution.

steps.label: Protect formation time
steps.text: Keep some work, especially for less experienced designers, done by hand so they practice critique and evaluation.

steps.label: Question the research
steps.text: Before citing a deskilling study, check whether its test conditions resemble how your designers actually work.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts are short and mostly opinion, so they give no direct measurement of skill change among working designers and do not show what the criticized research actually found.

briefings.title: Handing craft to AI: vendor claims versus tests
briefings.dek: Teams must decide how much design work to delegate to AI agents and models when vendor stories and independent tests point in different directions.
briefings.scenario: A design systems team at a large retailer is told to let an AI agent handle library updates, critique summaries, and first-draft specs so designers can focus on new features. Before changing their process, they have to decide whether the vendor's examples reflect what the tools will produce on their own screens.

positions.label: Delegate, keep judgment
positions.summary: Figma presents the agent as ready for general use. Its articles describe designers keeping the core product thinking while the agent does library updates, feedback gathering, and draft specs, and they cite teams at named companies as examples. Choosing what to hand off is framed as a skill in its own right.

positions.label: Independent tests disappoint
positions.summary: Hands-on writers tested new models on web and UI design. One concludes that Sonnet 5.5 falls short of the vendor's claims. Others compare models and effort settings, which suggests output quality depends on which model and setting you use rather than being reliably high.

briefings.context: Figma's posts come from the vendor and are about a product it has just made generally available. The UX Planet pieces are individual practitioner tests of general-purpose models, not of Figma's agent. The two sets cover different tools and different kinds of work, so they are not a direct comparison.

steps.label: Sort tasks
steps.text: List your recurring design tasks and mark which are mechanical, such as library updates and draft specs, and which depend on judgment.

steps.label: Run your own test
steps.text: Try a candidate tool on a real screen from your product, and compare the output with your own standards instead of the vendor's demonstration.

steps.label: Compare settings
steps.text: If you use a general-purpose model, test more than one model and more than one effort level before deciding where it fits.

briefings.caveat: The excerpts don't show the testing methods, scoring criteria, or results in detail, and none of them tests Figma's agent independently.
